titleText.es: Historia real (de Randall Munroe): tuve que hacer varios intentos para subir esta tira porque mi clave SSH estaba en la lista negra.
titleText.en: True story (from Randall Munroe): I had to make several attempts to upload this strip because my SSH key was blacklisted.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive explicitly identifies Randall Munroe in parentheses; the official English title text begins simply with ‘True story.’ Both versions refer to an SSH key affected by the real Debian OpenSSL weak-key incident.

regions.labelEs: SÓLO VOY A COMENTAR ESTAS LÍNEAS...

applications.explanationEn: Voy changes for the speaker, a links it to the planned action, and comentar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

excludedUnits.rationale: This is a commented programming-language function call and identifier sequence, not Spanish lexical text.
Although the identifier contains Spanish-looking pieces, the whole printed unit is a commented code identifier and call, not ordinary Spanish prose.
This entire printed unit is a commented programming identifier and function call, including the numeric abbreviation, rather than ordinary Spanish curriculum text.

regions.labelEs: DURANTE LA URGENCIA POR ARREGLAR EL FIASCO DE DEBIAN-OPENSSL, SE HAN DESCUBIERTO UNA SERIE DE AGUJEROS DE SEGURIDAD IMPORTANTES:

excludedUnits.rationale: Debian and OpenSSL are unchanged software-project names joined in the printed incident label, not Spanish lexical words.

applications.explanationEn: Han supplies the present form of haber for a plural reference, and descubierto is descubrir's irregular completed-action form.
Se leaves the discoverer unnamed, while han descubierto presents the discovery as completed and relevant now.
Agujeros is plural, de links the compound, and seguridad identifies the technical field in which the weaknesses exist.
Sistema names the thing, and the neutral descriptive adjective afectado follows it.
Although sistema ends in -a, it is masculine, so the matching singular adjective is afectado.

regions.labelEs: FEDORA CORE — VULNERABLE A CIERTO CIFRADO CÉSAR.

excludedUnits.rationale: Fedora Core is the unchanged proper name of a Linux distribution, not Spanish vocabulary.
César is the historical proper name retained inside the conventional cipher name, not a general Spanish vocabulary word.

applications.explanationEn: Vulnerable describes the system, a introduces the risk, and cierto cifrado names the particular cipher involved; the proper name remains visible but unscheduled.

regions.labelEs: XANDROS (EEE PC) — DA ACCESO ROOT SI SE LE PIDE CON VOZ FIRME.

excludedUnits.rationale: Xandros is the unchanged proper name of a Linux distribution, not Spanish vocabulary.
EEE PC is the unchanged commercial computer-model name in parentheses, not Spanish vocabulary.
Root is the unchanged Unix account label for the highest-privilege user, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Da is the present form of dar for the system, and acceso names what it grants.
Si introduces the possible condition, and pide remains an ordinary present-time form; se and le belong to the request construction between them.
Se leaves the requester unnamed, while pide supplies the present request action; le identifies the system receiving the request.
Voz names the thing, and the neutral descriptive adjective firme follows it.
Firme has one singular form for both genders, so it already matches the feminine singular noun voz.

excludedUnits.rationale: Gentoo is the unchanged proper name of a Linux distribution, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Vulnerable describes the system, a introduces the risk, and la adulación names that risk.

regions.labelEs: OLPC OS — VULNERABLE AL POWERBOOK DE JEFF GOLDBLUM.

excludedUnits.rationale: OLPC OS is the unchanged operating-system project label, not Spanish vocabulary.
PowerBook is the unchanged Apple product-family name, not Spanish vocabulary.
Jeff Goldblum is a person's proper name retained from the source joke, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.exampleEs: VULNERABLE AL POWERBOOK DE JEFF GOLDBLUM
applications.explanationEn: Vulnerable takes al before the named device, and de marks the device's owner; the product and personal names remain visible but unscheduled.

regions.labelEs: SLACKWARE — DA ACCESO ROOT SI EL USUARIO DICE "AMIGO" EN ÉLFICO.

excludedUnits.rationale: Slackware is the unchanged proper name of a Linux distribution, not Spanish vocabulary.
Root is the unchanged Unix account label for the highest-privilege user, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Da is the present form of dar for the system, and acceso names what it grants.

applications.exampleEs: SI EL USUARIO DICE "AMIGO" EN ÉLFICO
applications.explanationEn: Si introduces the possible condition, and dice stays in the ordinary present form; the intervening words state its subject and content.

regions.labelEs: UBUNTU — RESULTA QUE ESTA DISTRO NO ES MÁS QUE WINDOWS VISTA CON VARIOS TEMAS PERSONALIZADOS.

excludedUnits.rationale: Ubuntu is the unchanged proper name of a Linux distribution, not Spanish vocabulary.
Windows Vista is the unchanged commercial operating-system name, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Resulta frames a discovery, and que opens the information that has become clear.

applications.exampleEs: NO ES MÁS QUE WINDOWS VISTA CON VARIOS TEMAS PERSONALIZADOS
applications.explanationEn: No negates es, más que restricts the identification, and con varios temas personalizados completes the description of the excluded product name.
Temas names the software items, and the neutral descriptive adjective personalizados follows it.
Personalizados takes masculine plural -os to match temas.

cards.noteEn: The comic uses the formerly common accent in sólo. Current standard spelling normally writes solo without an accent when it means “only,” unless an accent is exceptionally needed to prevent genuine ambiguity.

example.en: I only need a minute.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir (“to go”), then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes to match the person: voy a means “I am going to,” vas a means “you are going to,” and va a means “he/she is going to.” The final action stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. This pattern expresses a plan, intention, or expected future event.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is going to do something?

example.en: I am going to study.

cards.answerEn: to (part of ir a + infinitive, going to do something)
to comment out; to disable a line of code by marking it as a comment
cards.noteEn: In programming, comentar can mean turning executable code into a comment so that the computer ignores it. This is more specific than ordinary comentar, ‘to comment on something.’

example.es: Voy a comentar esta línea mientras pruebo el programa.
example.en: I am going to comment out this line while I test the program.

cards.promptEs: fiasco de Debian-OpenSSL · agujeros de seguridad · sistemas vulnerables
cards.answerEn: the comic turns a real Debian OpenSSL weak-key incident into a list of absurd security flaws in other operating systems
cards.noteEn: Debian's 2008 OpenSSL vulnerability made cryptographic keys predictable and affected SSH keys, matching the title text about a blacklisted key. The left panels joke that essential safeguards were commented out; the table then invents vulnerabilities based on stereotypes, fantasy references, and software reputations.
Urgencia can name either the need to act quickly or the urgent situation causing that pressure.

example.en: They fixed the fault urgently.

cards.answerEn: to; connects an urgency or rush to the action prompting it
cards.noteEn: After a noun such as urgencia or prisa, por can introduce the action someone is eager or pressed to complete. Natural English often uses ‘to’ instead of translating por as ‘for.’

example.en: There was a rush to finish.

cards.noteEn: A fiasco is a conspicuous failure, especially one involving confusion, poor planning, or public embarrassment.

example.en: The launch was a fiasco.

cards.answerEn: marks an action whose doer is not named
cards.noteEn: Before a third-person verb, se can focus on what happens rather than who does it. English often uses a passive form such as ‘is requested’ or ‘have been discovered.’

example.en: Several errors were found.

cards.promptEs: se + verbo en tercera persona (sin nombrar quién actúa)
cards.questionEn: How can Spanish focus on an action or result without naming who does it?
cards.answerEn: Put se before a third-person verb and state what happens; the person doing it can remain unnamed.
cards.noteEn: English often uses a passive form. Spanish may use se with a simple verb or with a completed construction such as se han encontrado. Other uses of se follow different patterns.

example.en: The results were published.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.answerEn: discovered; found (completed-action form used after haber)
cards.noteEn: Descubierto is the irregular completed-action form of descubrir. After a form of haber, it stays unchanged: he descubierto, han descubierto, and so on.

example.en: They have discovered a new error.

cards.noteEn: Una serie de introduces a related group or succession of people, things, or events.

example.en: There was a series of problems.

cards.questionEn: How do you name a weakness that can be exploited in a system?
cards.answerEn: Say agujero de seguridad; use agujeros de seguridad for more than one.
cards.noteEn: The expression literally uses ‘hole of security,’ while natural English puts the field first: ‘security hole.’ Vulnerabilidad de seguridad is another common technical term.

example.es: El parche corrige un agujero de seguridad.
example.en: The patch fixes a security hole.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links a hole or problem to the field of security
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses de in compounds such as agujero de seguridad and problema de seguridad. English normally puts ‘security’ directly before the other noun.

example.en: They found a security problem.

cards.noteEn: Importante has the same masculine and feminine singular form. The plural importantes ends in -es.

example.en: Several important matters remain.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Afectado describes a masculine singular person or thing that experiences the effect of a problem or event.

example.en: The affected system is disconnected.

cards.answerEn: vulnerable; open to harm or attack
cards.noteEn: Vulnerable has the same form for masculine and feminine singular nouns. Use vulnerable a before the danger or influence involved.

example.es: El servidor es vulnerable a ese ataque.
example.en: The server is vulnerable to that attack.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what danger or influence something is vulnerable to?
cards.answerEn: Use vulnerable a before the danger; a and el combine as al.
cards.noteEn: The describing word vulnerable stays the same in masculine and feminine singular. Its complement begins with a, even when English uses ‘to.’

example.es: Este material es vulnerable al agua.
example.en: This material is vulnerable to water.

cards.answerEn: to; introduces the danger after vulnerable
cards.noteEn: The adjective vulnerable normally takes a before the attack, influence, or problem that can cause harm.

example.es: La planta es vulnerable al frío.
example.en: The plant is vulnerable to the cold.

cards.noteEn: As a noun, cifrado can name a method or system for encoding information. The verb cifrar means ‘to encrypt’ or ‘to encode.’

example.es: Este cifrado es fácil de romper.
example.en: This cipher is easy to break.

cards.answerEn: a simple substitution cipher that shifts every letter by the same fixed number of positions
cards.noteEn: The method is associated with Julius Caesar. Because there are very few possible shifts, it is easy to test every key; calling a modern operating system vulnerable to it is intentionally absurd.
Da is the present form of dar used with one other person or thing. In technical contexts, dar acceso means ‘to grant access.’

example.es: La tarjeta da acceso al edificio.
example.en: The card grants access to the building.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something grants or provides access?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of dar followed by acceso; use a before the place, system, or resource when it is stated.
cards.noteEn: The form of dar changes with the subject: da acceso, dan acceso, dio acceso, and so on.

example.es: La llave da acceso al almacén.
example.en: The key grants access to the warehouse.

cards.answerEn: access; entry; permission to use something
cards.noteEn: Acceso can refer to physical entry or permission to use a system, account, or resource.

example.es: No tengo acceso a esa cuenta.
example.en: I do not have access to that account.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce a real or possible condition with “if”?
cards.answerEn: Use si without an accent, followed by an ordinary present-time verb form.
cards.noteEn: This pattern treats the condition as genuinely possible. Spanish normally does not put a future-tense verb directly after si in this kind of condition; the result can appear separately as a statement, prediction, or command.

example.en: If you have time, call.

cards.answerEn: may have no separate English word; marks the thing receiving the effect
cards.noteEn: Le can appear before a verb even when a later phrase beginning with a names the receiver explicitly. English normally states that receiver only once.

example.es: Le cambié la rueda al coche.
example.en: I changed the car's wheel.

cards.noteEn: Pide is the present form of pedir used with one other person or thing. With passive se, se pide focuses on what is requested rather than who requests it.

example.en: A password is requested.

cards.noteEn: When firme describes a voice or tone, it means controlled, confident, and not yielding. This is different from merely saying that a hand or object does not shake.

example.en: She answered in a firm voice.

cards.noteEn: Adulación is exaggerated praise used to please or influence someone.

example.es: No se dejó convencer por la adulación.
example.en: He was not persuaded by flattery.

cards.answerEn: a reference to Independence Day, where Jeff Goldblum's character uses a PowerBook to help upload a virus to the alien mothership
cards.noteEn: The comic turns that film scene into a mock software vulnerability: merely encountering the named laptop supposedly threatens the operating system.
Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.

example.en: I’m going to the market.

cards.answerEn: belonging to; often expressed with ’s in English
cards.noteEn: De can connect a thing to its owner. Spanish says el libro de Ana where English can say ‘Ana’s book.’

example.en: It is Luis's computer.

cards.noteEn: Usuario is a person who uses a service, device, or computer account. The feminine form is usuaria.

example.en: Each user has a password.

cards.answerEn: a reference to the Doors of Durin in The Lord of the Rings, opened by saying mellon, the Elvish word for “friend”
cards.noteEn: The comic reimagines the fantasy door's spoken solution as a laughably weak computer-access rule.
Amigo can identify a male friend or appear as the masculine dictionary form when discussing the word itself.

example.en: Pablo is a good friend.

cards.answerEn: Elvish; relating to elves or an elf language
cards.noteEn: Élfico can describe something associated with fantasy elves. Used after en, it can name an Elvish language.

example.es: La inscripción está escrita en élfico.
example.en: The inscription is written in Elvish.

cards.noteEn: Resulta que introduces information that has just been discovered, is surprising, or changes the listener's understanding.

example.es: Resulta que la tienda está cerrada.
example.en: It turns out that the store is closed.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce a surprising fact that has just become clear?
cards.answerEn: Use resulta que, then state the newly revealed information.
cards.noteEn: Resulta que often corresponds to ‘it turns out that.’ It frames the next statement as a discovery or correction to what someone expected.

example.en: It turns out that they already knew each other.

cards.answerEn: that; introduces what turns out to be true
cards.noteEn: After resulta, que opens the newly revealed statement. Learn resulta que together as ‘it turns out that.’

example.en: It turns out that you were right.

cards.noteEn: Distro is informal technical shorthand for distribución, especially a packaged version of an operating system such as a Linux distribution.

example.es: Probé una distro diferente de Linux.
example.en: I tried a different Linux distribution.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is nothing but, or only, a particular thing?
cards.answerEn: Use no, a form of ser, then más que and the thing or description that remains.
cards.noteEn: Ser means “to be” and changes for time and subject: no es más que, no era más que, no fue más que. Más que normally introduces a comparison, but inside this negative frame it restricts the subject to only what follows.

example.es: La llamada no fue más que una broma.
example.en: The call was nothing but a joke.

cards.answerEn: no more than; only (as part of no ser más que)
cards.noteEn: Más normally means “more.” Between a negative form of ser and que, it helps restrict something to the description that follows.

example.es: No fue más que un error.
example.en: It was nothing more than a mistake.

cards.answerEn: than; no separate word in the full expression “nothing but”
cards.noteEn: In no ser más que, que completes the restriction introduced by más. The form of ser changes for the person and time.

example.es: Eso no es más que una idea.
example.en: That is nothing but an idea.

cards.noteEn: Varios before a plural noun means more than one, usually an unspecified small number or range.

example.en: We tried several designs.

cards.noteEn: In software, a tema is a coordinated set of colors, images, and styles that changes how an interface looks. In other contexts, tema can mean ‘topic.’

example.es: La aplicación incluye varios temas oscuros.
example.en: The application includes several dark themes.

cards.noteEn: Personalizados describes masculine plural things adapted to a particular person, purpose, or preference.

example.en: We sell custom designs.
